transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I'm here because... well, it's been going on for nearly two years now. I'm absolutely sure the contractor we hired and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They're keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. And you know, kitchens are so important. I remember when I was a little girl, my mother's kitchen was the heart of the house. She had this beautiful yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. I always wanted a kitchen like that, warm and inviting. But anyway, no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many excuses they all give, I know what they're doing. They think I don't see it, but I do. My husband, bless him, he just doesn't understand. He bought me this lovely set of mixing bowls for my birthday last year, blue ceramic, just gorgeous, but I can't even enjoy using them in that kitchen. They're all in on it, I just know it.
During times when this has been happening, have you also had periods where you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep?

Unusually energetic? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I definitely need my sleep. I usually get my eight hours, well, unless Arthur's snoring wakes me up. He sounds like a broken lawnmower sometimes, bless him. We actually bought a new mattress last year to see if it would help him sleep quieter, one of those thick memory foam ones? The salesman at the furniture store was so pushy about it. He was a young man, wore far too much cologne. I really can't stand strong cologne, it just lingers in the air forever. My father used to wear Old Spice, and that was just a nice, clean, subtle smell, you know? But this young man at the store smelled like a whole department store counter... anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, sleep. No, I don't have times where I'm bursting with energy or staying up all night. I just go to bed at my regular time.
Have you ever heard voices when no one else was there?

Voices? No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear anything that isn't there. Although, speaking of hearing things, the walls in our house are so terribly thin. We bought the place back in '82, and it's a lovely split-level, but you can hear every little thing from the street. The neighbor's dog, a little terrier mix, barks at absolutely every car that goes by. Yap, yap, yap, all afternoon. I tried talking to Susan about it—she's the owner, a nice enough woman, makes a wonderful pecan pie for the block party every summer—but she just says he's 'protecting the house.' Protecting it from the mailman, I suppose! The mailman we have now is always running late, too. Not like Mr. Henderson from when my kids were little. You could set your watch by Mr. Henderson. But no, I don't hear voices or anything strange like that. Just the usual neighborhood racket.
Has anyone told you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one topic to another?

Hard to follow? Well, Arthur tells me I talk a lot, but husbands always say that, don't they? He's always been a man of few words. When we first started dating, I thought he was just mysterious, you know? We met at a church social, and he just stood by the punch bowl, looking so handsome in his brown suit. They don't make suits like that anymore, the fabric was so sturdy. Now everything you buy at the department store is so thin, it falls apart after three washes. I bought a blouse at Macy's last month, a lovely peach color—peach always washes me out a little, but I liked the collar—and the button popped right off the first time I wore it. I had to dig through my sewing tin to find a match, and you know how impossible it is to find the exact right shade of thread. My grandmother had this huge collection of thread on wooden spools. Wooden spools! You never see those anymore... but no, nobody has ever told me I'm hard to understand. I speak perfectly clearly, if you ask me. I just have a lot to say.
During this time, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, everyone gets a little blue sometimes, especially in the winter. The winters here feel so much longer than they used to. I remember when the kids were young, we'd get a good snow in December and it was just magical. We had this old wooden toboggan, the kind with the curled front? Arthur spent a whole weekend sanding and varnishing it one year. He was always so good with his hands. He built a birdhouse for the backyard, too, painted it a bright robin's egg blue. The blue jays absolutely loved it, but the squirrels, oh my goodness, the squirrels would just hang upside down and steal all the suet. We tried everything to keep them away—greasing the pole, putting little baffles on it—but those creatures are like acrobats. I saw a special on PBS once about how smart squirrels actually are, they can solve puzzles and remember where they hid nuts for months. Isn't that incredible? I can barely remember where I put my reading glasses half the time! I had a lovely pair with little rhinestones on the corners, but I left them at the grocery store checkout last Tuesday. The cashier was a new girl, very sweet, but she bagged my bread under a heavy bottle of laundry detergent. It was completely squished by the time I got home. But no, I haven't been depressed for two weeks or anything like that. Just the normal ups and downs, you know.
Have you been diagnosed with any brain or neurological illness?

Brain illness? No, no, I've never had anything wrong with my brain. Thank goodness for that. My memory is sharp as a tack, except for the reading glasses, of course. My Aunt Clara, though, she had terrible trouble with her memory toward the end. We had to move her into one of those assisted living places over in Westbridge. It was a very nice facility, they had a beautiful garden with these big, blooming hydrangea bushes. I've always wanted to grow hydrangeas, but the soil in our yard is just too acidic. I read in a magazine—Better Homes and Gardens, I think it was, or maybe Southern Living—that you can change the color of the blooms by putting coffee grounds or rusty nails in the dirt. Isn't that funny? Rusty nails! Arthur used to keep coffee cans full of rusty nails and screws in the garage. He never threw anything away, said you never know when you might need a two-inch wood screw. When we finally cleaned out the garage last spring, we found things we hadn't seen since 1990. We even found the old croquet set we used to play with on the Fourth of July. The kids would get so competitive, especially my son, David. He always had to have the blue mallet. He was so particular, even as a little boy. He wouldn't eat his peas if they touched his mashed potatoes. I had to buy those special plates with the little dividers in them. But no, no brain problems for me. Just regular doctor checkups, that's all.
Do you believe anyone is controlling your thoughts?

Controlling my thoughts? Goodness, no, nobody can do that. That sounds like something out of one of those science fiction movies my grandson likes to watch. He came over last weekend and had me sit through this whole film about people living in a computer simulation. It was so loud, all explosions and flashing lights. I told him, "Tommy, my ears are ringing!" He just laughed. He's such a sweet boy, though. He's starting college in the fall, going all the way up to State. I can hardly believe it. It feels like just yesterday he was running around the backyard catching fireflies in a mason jar. We used to poke holes in the lid with an ice pick so they could breathe. You have to be so careful with an ice pick, Arthur always warned me about that. He had an uncle who actually punctured his own hand trying to chip ice for a punch bowl back in the fifties. Can you imagine? They didn't have those fancy refrigerators with the ice makers built right into the door back then. My neighbor, Susan, just remodeled her kitchen and she got one of those refrigerators. Stainless steel, she calls it, but I swear it shows every single fingerprint. I told her, "Susan, you're going to be wiping that thing down three times a day." She's always cleaning, that woman. I think she vacuums her driveway. But no, nobody is putting thoughts in my head or controlling them or anything silly like that. My thoughts are my own.
Have you started any new medicines around the time these beliefs began?

New medicines? Let me think... no, no new pills or anything like that. I've been taking the same blood pressure pill for, oh, it must be five years now. Dr. Evans prescribed it right before he retired. Such a shame he retired, he had the best bedside manner. His office always smelled like peppermint, he kept a bowl of those little red and white striped candies on his desk. The ones wrapped in clear plastic? I used to take two, one for me and one for Arthur. Arthur loved peppermints, he said they settled his stomach after dinner. We used to have pot roast every Sunday, with carrots and potatoes roasted right in the pan juices. I'd make a gravy from scratch, none of that powdered stuff from a packet. My mother taught me how to make a proper roux. You have to stir it constantly or it burns, and once it burns, you just have to throw the whole thing out and start over. It takes patience, which is something young people just don't seem to have these days. Everything is microwave this and instant that. I saw a commercial the other day for a machine that makes a whole cup of coffee in thirty seconds. Thirty seconds! Where's the joy in that? I still use my old percolator. It makes this wonderful bubbling sound in the morning, it's so comforting. But no, to answer your question, I haven't started any new medications. Just the same old routine.
Have you become less interested in spending time with other people than you used to be?

Less interested? Oh, no, not at all. Outside of dealing with the remodel, I still keep up with my church gatherings, my book club, all my household routines, and family plans the way I usually do. I wouldn't miss book club for the world. We're reading that new mystery novel, the one set in the English countryside? The author describes the gardens so beautifully, it makes me want to plant roses. I tried growing roses once, those lovely climbing ones, but the aphids got to them. Just covered the stems, little green bugs everywhere. I tried spraying them with soapy water, which is what my neighbor Susan told me to do. She swears by Dawn dish soap for everything. She even uses it to get grease stains out of her husband's work shirts. He works down at the auto body shop on Main Street. He's the one who fixed the dent in my bumper when I backed into that mailbox last winter. The snow was piled so high, I just didn't see it! It was a terrible sound, that crunch. The postmaster was very understanding about it, though. He said it happens at least three times a winter on that route. But anyway, yes, I still see everyone just the same. I'm as busy as ever.
Have other people told you that you go off track when you talk?

Off track? I don't think so. I mean, my daughter sometimes tells me I talk too much when she's trying to get the kids ready for school, but she's just always in a rush. Those mornings are so chaotic at her house. The youngest, little Lily, she refuses to wear anything but purple. Every single day, it has to be purple. We went shopping for her birthday last month, and we had to go to three different stores just to find a purple winter coat. It’s hard to find a good coat these days that isn’t too bulky, you know? You want them to be warm, but if it’s too thick, they can’t even bend their arms. It looks like they’re little snowmen waddling around. When my children were little, I used to knit their sweaters. I made this beautiful cable-knit cardigan for my son—it took me three months! I used this lovely forest green yarn I found at a little shop downtown that closed years ago. It’s a shame how many local shops have closed down. There used to be a wonderful bakery on the corner that made the best eclairs. The custard inside was just perfect, not too sweet. But no, nobody has ever told me I go off track. I just like to share stories.
Before these concerns about the contractor began, did you have a significant head injury?

A head injury? Oh, goodness, no. I've always been very careful, well, except for that time I slipped on the ice outside the grocery store, but I just bruised my hip then. Ice is so treacherous around here. The city really doesn't salt the sidewalks enough, if you ask me. I remember one winter, it must have been '98, the ice storm was so bad the power was out for three days. We had to bring all the perishables out to the garage just to keep them cold. And we huddled around the fireplace in the living room, wrapped in every blanket we owned. My husband built this roaring fire, and we actually toasted marshmallows right there in the house. It felt like camping, but without the mosquitoes. I can't stand mosquitoes. They always seem to bite me more than anyone else. My sister says it's because I eat too many bananas, but I don't know if I believe that. She reads all sorts of strange things in those magazines she gets at the checkout line. The ones with the big bold headlines about aliens and celebrities. I just buy the ones with the recipes. There was a lovely recipe for a lemon pound cake in one last month, but I haven't gotten around to baking it because of all this mess with the house. But no, to answer you, I haven't hit my head or had any injuries like that.
Have you found that it’s harder than it used to be to feel emotions, such as joy or sadness?

Harder to feel emotions? Oh, no, I feel everything just as much as I always have. I still get so happy when I see my grandchildren, and I certainly get upset about this whole mess with the house. Honestly, sometimes I think I feel things too strongly, like when I watch those commercials on television with the sad animals in the shelters. The ones with that Sarah McLachlan song playing in the background? They just break my heart. I always have to change the channel or I'll start crying right there in the living room. I love animals, you know. We had a golden retriever named Buster when the kids were growing up. He was the sweetest dog, just a big goofball. He used to chase his own tail until he'd get dizzy and fall over on the rug. That rug was a nightmare to keep clean, though. It was a cream color, which was a terrible mistake with a dog and three kids. I spent half my life on my hands and knees with a bottle of carpet cleaner, scrubbing out mud and spilled juice. Kids always seem to spill the brightest colored drinks, don't they? Fruit punch, grape juice... it's never just water. I remember one time my son spilled a whole pitcher of cherry Kool-Aid during a birthday party. We ended up having to put a big armchair over the stain. It actually looked quite nice in that corner, now that I think about it. But no, my emotions are perfectly fine. I feel things just like I always have.
Aside from the situation with the contractor and your neighbors, do you believe other people are trying to harm or cheat you?

Harm me? No, no, it's really just the contractor and those neighbors who are in on it. I don't go around thinking the whole world is out to get me, I'm not crazy. I mean, the mailman is perfectly nice, he always waves when he drops off the letters. Although, the mail service isn't what it used to be, is it? Sometimes my magazines come a week late, and the edges are all bent. I hate when the pages are creased before I even get to read them. I subscribe to this lovely gardening magazine, *Better Homes and Gardens*, I've been getting it for, oh, thirty years now. They had this wonderful spread last month on growing hydrangeas. I tried to grow hydrangeas in the front yard a few years ago, but the soil here is just too alkaline. They turned out this pale, washed-out pink instead of that beautiful deep blue. You have to add aluminum sulfate to the soil to get the blue color, but I always forget to buy it when I'm at the garden center. The garden center on Elm Street is so nice, though, they have this big orange cat that just sleeps on the bags of potting soil all day. I love cats, but my husband was allergic, so we could only ever have dogs. Buster, the golden retriever I told you about, he was terrified of cats anyway. One time a stray cat hissed at him from the top of the fence, and Buster hid under the porch for three hours. We had to coax him out with a piece of sliced ham. Ham is getting so expensive at the deli counter lately, have you noticed? But anyway, no, I don't think anyone else is trying to cheat me or anything like that. Just the people involved with the house.
Did your family notice a clear change in your personality around the time these beliefs started?

A change in my personality? Oh, goodness, no. My kids and my sister, they'd tell you I'm exactly the same woman I've always been. I mean, my sister Linda might say I'm stubborn, but she's been saying that since we were little girls sharing a bedroom. We had this awful floral wallpaper in that room... big yellow and orange daisies. It was the seventies, I suppose, so everything was yellow and orange and avocado green. 

I actually still have an avocado green mixing bowl in my kitchen, believe it or not. It belonged to our mother. I use it every single time I make potato salad. My potato salad is always a big hit at the Fourth of July barbecue. Well, it used to be, before all this nonsense with the neighbors started, anyway. I put just a little bit of sweet pickle relish in it—that's the secret, you see. Some people use dill, but dill just completely overpowers the mayonnaise, if you ask me. I accidentally bought dill pickles once when they were on sale, and my husband wouldn't even touch them. He was so picky about his sandwiches. He had to have the crusts cut off his toast until the day he passed, bless his heart. 

But no, to get back to what you were saying... I haven't changed at all. I'm just me.
Do you believe the contractor or your neighbors can send you special messages through things like the television, radio, or newspaper?

Messages through the television? Goodness, no, that sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. Like that show my grandson watches, the one with the aliens and the spaceships... *Doctor Who*, I think it's called? He tried to explain it to me once, about a police box that's bigger on the inside, but I just couldn't wrap my head around it. I prefer the older shows, the ones that make sense. *Murder, She Wrote* is my absolute favorite. Angela Lansbury was just so elegant, wasn't she? I used to have a typewriter just like the one she used in the opening credits. It was a heavy old Royal typewriter, black with those round glass keys. It weighed an absolute ton. I used it to type up all my recipes before personal computers became a thing. 

Now everything is on the computer or the phone. My daughter got me one of those iPads for Christmas last year, and I still barely know how to use it. I mostly just use it to play Solitaire and look up knitting patterns. I'm trying to knit a sweater for my newest granddaughter, but the yarn I bought is so fuzzy, it's hard to see the stitches. It's a beautiful lavender color, though. Lavender always reminds me of my grandmother's house. She used to keep little sachets of dried lavender in all her dresser drawers to keep the moths away. It smelled so much nicer than those awful mothballs. 

But no, the television is just for watching my shows and the evening news. Nobody is sending me secret messages through it or the newspaper. The only thing I get from the newspaper is ink on my fingers, and I always have to wash my hands right after I read it.
Has a doctor ever told you that a physical illness was causing these beliefs?

A physical illness? No, no doctor has ever said anything like that to me. I'm healthy as a horse, honestly. I mean, my blood pressure is a little high, but Dr. Evans says that's just because of my age, and he gave me a little white pill for it. I take it every morning with my tea. I always have a cup of Earl Grey tea first thing, with just a splash of milk. My mother used to drink it with lemon, but I always thought the lemon made it too tart. She had this beautiful china tea set, delicate little cups with tiny pink roses painted on them. I think my sister Linda has it now. Linda always was the one who ended up with all the nice family heirlooms. I got the avocado green bowl, like I said, and a box of old photographs. 

Those photographs are lovely, though. I spent a whole weekend last winter just organizing them into albums. There's one picture of my husband and me on our honeymoon in Florida... we went to Daytona Beach. It rained for three days straight, but we still had a wonderful time. We just stayed in the hotel and played gin rummy. He was terrible at card games, he always gave away his hand with his face. If he had a good hand, his left eyebrow would go up, just a fraction of an inch. It was the cutest thing. 

But anyway, no, no physical illnesses causing anything. I'm perfectly healthy, aside from the blood pressure. And maybe a little arthritis in my knees when it rains, but that's just getting older, isn't it?
Have you ever seen things that other people could not see?

Seen things? Oh, no, my eyesight is perfectly fine, thank goodness. Well, I do wear reading glasses, of course. I have them scattered all over the house—one pair by the armchair in the living room, one on my nightstand, one in the kitchen next to the recipe box. They're those little half-moon ones, you know? I bought a three-pack at the pharmacy because I'm always misplacing them. Just last Tuesday, I spent twenty minutes looking for a pair, and they were sitting right on top of my head the whole time! My neighbor, Mrs. Gable—not the ones causing all the trouble, the nice lady on the other side—she laughed so hard when I told her. 

Mrs. Gable has a beautiful garden, by the way. Her hydrangeas are just spectacular this year. They're that deep, vibrant blue. She says the secret is putting coffee grounds in the soil to change the acidity, but I tried that once and all I got was a bunch of ants. Ants are such a nuisance, especially in the summer. They always find their way into the kitchen if you leave even a speck of sugar on the counter. I had to buy those little plastic traps, the ones you hide under the sink. My husband used to just spray that awful-smelling bug spray everywhere, but I couldn't stand the smell of it. It lingered for days. 

But no, I don't see things that aren't there or anything like that. Just my regular old living room and Mrs. Gable's hydrangeas out the window.
When these concerns about the contractor first started, did you also have any fever?

A fever? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I haven't had a real fever since... oh, it must have been the winter of '98. Or was it '99? We had that terrible ice storm that knocked the power out for three days. My husband and I had to bundle up in layers and sleep in the living room right next to the fireplace. We dragged the mattress right off the bed and onto the floor. It was actually sort of romantic, in a freezing-to-death sort of way. We roasted hot dogs on sticks right in the living room! I remember we ran out of firewood by the second day and my husband had to chop up an old wooden chair we had in the basement. It was a rickety old thing anyway, missing a rung, so it wasn't a great loss. 

I bought a replacement chair at a yard sale a few years later. It had a lovely floral cushion, very spring-like. I always loved yard sales, you never know what treasures you'll find. I once found a beautiful set of silver spoons for only two dollars! They just needed a good polish. Polishing silver is such a soothing chore, don't you think? It's very satisfying to see the tarnish rub away and the shine come through. 

But no, no fever when all this business with the contractor started. I was feeling perfectly fine, physically anyway.
Has anyone ever told you that your thoughts seem jumbled or that you stop making sense when you talk?

Jumbled? No, I don't think so. I mean, my daughter Sarah sometimes tells me to get to the point, but she's always in such a rush. Young people these days are always rushing, aren't they? Rush, rush, rush. She works in marketing, always on her phone, even when we're having lunch. We went to that new Italian place downtown last week, the one with the red and white checkered tablecloths. It reminded me of a place my husband and I used to go to when we were first dating. They had the most wonderful garlic bread, just dripping with butter. 

I tried to make garlic bread like that once at home, but I burned it to a crisp. The smoke alarm went off, and it was one of those old ones that you couldn't just press a button to silence. You had to take the battery out, and I couldn't reach it! I had to stand on a kitchen chair, and I was waving a dish towel at it like a madwoman. The dog was barking... oh, we had a golden retriever back then named Buster. He was such a good boy, but terrified of loud noises. Whenever there was a thunderstorm, he'd hide under the bed and wouldn't come out for hours. I used to have to coax him out with little pieces of cheese. He loved sharp cheddar. 

But anyway, no, nobody has said I stop making sense. I think I make perfect sense, I just have a lot to say sometimes.
Has anyone who knows you well ever said that your thinking has become disorganized?

Disorganized? Oh, certainly not my thinking. Now, if you want to talk about disorganized, you should have seen my hall closet last weekend! I finally decided to tackle it, and oh my goodness, it was a complete disaster area. I pulled out things I haven't seen in years. I found our old Scrabble board tucked right at the very back under a pile of heavy winter coats. 

We used to play Scrabble every single Sunday evening when the kids were little. My husband always insisted on keeping score, he was very particular about the math. He used this little green spiral notebook. I actually found that notebook, too! It had a grocery list tucked inside from... oh, it must have been 1992. Bread was so much cheaper back then. I usually buy the whole wheat kind now, the one with the little oats baked right onto the crust. It makes the most wonderful toast. I have a slice every morning with my tea and a bit of orange marmalade. I tried making my own marmalade from scratch once, but boiling the rinds takes simply forever and it just made the entire kitchen sticky. My slippers were practically glued to the linoleum! So now I just buy the glass jar with the little gingham lid at the supermarket. It's much easier. 

But no, nobody has ever told me my thinking is disorganized. I keep everything perfectly straight up here.

patient.answer: Well, I'm here because... well, it's been going on for nearly two years now. I'm absolutely sure the contractor we hired and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They're keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. And you know, kitchens are so important. I remember when I was a little girl, my mother's kitchen was the heart of the house. She had this beautiful yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. I always wanted a kitchen like that, warm and inviting. But anyway, no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many excuses they all give, I know what they're doing. They think I don't see it, but I do. My husband, bless him, he just doesn't understand. He bought me this lovely set of mixing bowls for my birthday last year, blue ceramic, just gorgeous, but I can't even enjoy using them in that kitchen. They're all in on it, I just know it.

doctor.question: During times when this has been happening, have you also had periods where you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep?

patient.answer: Unusually energetic? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I definitely need my sleep. I usually get my eight hours, well, unless Arthur's snoring wakes me up. He sounds like a broken lawnmower sometimes, bless him. We actually bought a new mattress last year to see if it would help him sleep quieter, one of those thick memory foam ones? The salesman at the furniture store was so pushy about it. He was a young man, wore far too much cologne. I really can't stand strong cologne, it just lingers in the air forever. My father used to wear Old Spice, and that was just a nice, clean, subtle smell, you know? But this young man at the store smelled like a whole department store counter... anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, sleep. No, I don't have times where I'm bursting with energy or staying up all night. I just go to bed at my regular time.

We used to play Scrabble every single Sunday evening when the kids were little. My husband always insisted on keeping score, he was very particular about the math. He used this little green spiral notebook. I actually found that notebook, too! It had a grocery list tucked inside from... oh, it must have been 1992. Bread was so much cheaper back then. I usually buy the whole wheat kind now, the one with the little oats baked right onto the crust. It makes the most wonderful toast. I have a slice every morning with my tea and a bit of orange marmalade. I tried making my own marmalade from scratch once, but boiling the rinds takes simply forever and it just made the entire kitchen sticky. My slippers were practically glued to the linoleum! So now I just buy the glass jar with the little gingham lid at the supermarket. It's much easier. 

But no, nobody has ever told me my thinking is disorganized. I keep everything perfectly straight up here.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a persistent, non-bizarre persecutory delusion lasting nearly two years, focused specifically on the contractor and some neighbors cheating her. She denies hallucinations, thought insertion/control, ideas of reference, negative symptoms, mood episodes, and there is no evidence of schizophrenia-spectrum disorganization causing marked global deterioration. No medical/neurological illness, head injury, fever, or medication change suggests an organic psychosis. This pattern is most consistent with persistent delusional disorder.
